title: How Virtual Works — vtables
summary: Ordinary calls are resolved at **compile time** (early binding). Virtual calls are resolved at **run time** (late binding) through a hidden pointer in each object, the `vptr`, to a per-class table of function addresses, the `vtable`. The cost is one pointer per object and one indirection per call.
markdown:
## Early and late binding ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Early["Early binding: an ordinary call"] direction LR E1["obj.f()"] -->|"the compiler emits a call
to a fixed address"| E2["f"] end subgraph Late["Late binding: a virtual call"] direction LR L1["ref.f()"] -->|"read the object's vptr"| L2["that class's vtable"] -->|"read the slot for f"| L3["call that address"] end ``` | | Binding | Decided | |---|---|---| | Non-virtual call | Early (static) | By the compiler | | Virtual call | Late (dynamic) | While the program runs | The standard does not say how virtual dispatch must be implemented. Every mainstream compiler uses the mechanism below. ## The vtable ```cpp class Animal { public: virtual ~Animal() = default; virtual void speak() const; virtual void move() const; }; class Dog : public Animal { public: void speak() const override; // move is not overridden }; class Cat : public Animal { public: void speak() const override; void move() const override; }; ``` ``` OBJECTS VTABLES: one per CLASS, shared by all its objects ┌────────────┐ Dog's vtable │ rex (Dog) │ ┌──────────────┬──────────────────┐ │ vptr ──────┼──────────▶ │ slot 0 dtor │ ~Dog │ │ members │ │ slot 1 speak │ Dog::speak │ overridden └────────────┘ │ slot 2 move │ Animal::move │ inherited └──────────────┴──────────────────┘ ┌────────────┐ Cat's vtable │ tom (Cat) │ ┌──────────────┬──────────────────┐ │ vptr ──────┼──────────▶ │ slot 0 dtor │ ~Cat │ │ members │ │ slot 1 speak │ Cat::speak │ └────────────┘ │ slot 2 move │ Cat::move │ └──────────────┴──────────────────┘ ``` | Piece | Where | Holds | |---|---|---| | **vtable** | One per class with virtual functions | The address of that class's version of each virtual function | | **vptr** | One hidden member in every object of such a class | The address of its class's vtable | Every class in a hierarchy uses the same slot number for the same function. So `animalRef.speak()` compiles to three steps that work without knowing the dynamic type: 1. Read the object's `vptr`. 2. Read slot 1 of the table it points to. 3. Call the address found there. ## The cost | | Cost | |---|---| | Memory per object | One pointer, 8 bytes on a 64-bit system, plus any padding | | Memory per class | One table | | Time per call | Two extra memory reads and an indirect call | | Lost optimisation | The compiler generally **cannot inline** a virtual call, which is often the larger effect | ```cpp struct NoVirtual { int x; }; // sizeof is 4 struct HasVirtual { int x; virtual ~HasVirtual() = default; }; // sizeof is 16: an 8-byte vptr, the int, and 4 bytes of padding ``` In most code this is immaterial. It becomes measurable when a tiny virtual function is called millions of times in a tight loop over small objects. Alternatives for those cases: | Alternative | Lesson | |---|---| | Compile-time polymorphism with CRTP | [[11.05 CRTP, Mixins and Static Polymorphism]] | | A closed set of types in a `std::variant` | [[10.04 stdoptional, stdvariant, stdany and stdtuple]] | | Grouping objects by type and processing each group in bulk | [[13.04 Performance, Caches and Data-Oriented Design]] | ## Devirtualization When the compiler can prove the dynamic type, it replaces the virtual call with a direct one, which can then be inlined. This is **devirtualization**. | Situation | Why the type is known | |---|---| | A call on a local object by value | Its type is exactly the declared one | | The class or the function is `final` | Nothing can override further | | Whole-program optimisation shows a single implementation | There is only one candidate | Marking leaf classes `final` is therefore a small, free optimisation. ## Why virtual calls in constructors do not dispatch The `vptr` is set by each constructor in turn. ``` constructing a Dog: Animal's constructor runs vptr points at Animal's vtable Dog's constructor runs vptr points at Dog's vtable ``` While `Animal`'s constructor is running, the object **is** an `Animal`: the `Dog` members are not yet constructed. A virtual call at that moment reaches `Animal`'s version, which is the only safe choice. Destruction mirrors it: by the time `~Animal` runs, the `Dog` part has already been destroyed and the `vptr` has been set back. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? How many vtables exist for a class that has 1,000 objects? - 1,000, one per object + One - One per virtual function - None until a virtual function is called > The vtable is per class. Each object holds its own vptr, and all of them point at that single table. ? What is late binding? - Calling a function after the object is destroyed - Linking a library after the program has started + Choosing the function to call at run time, by dynamic type - Defining a function after it is first called > Early binding fixes the function while compiling. Late binding looks it up through the vptr while running. ? Why does adding five more virtual functions not increase `sizeof` the class? - Because virtual functions are stored on the heap + They add vtable slots; each object still has one vptr - Because `sizeof` ignores functions and pointers - It does; each adds 8 bytes > The extra function pointers live in the shared table, not in every object. ? Besides the indirection, what is the main performance cost of a virtual call? - It allocates memory on every call - It copies the object - It always causes a cache miss + The compiler usually cannot inline it > Without knowing the target, the compiler cannot inline the call or optimise across it. Devirtualization recovers this when the type is known. ```
ideas:
1. Print `sizeof` a class before adding a virtual function, after adding one, and after adding five.
2. In a Release build, time 100 million calls to a plain member function and to a virtual one. Is the difference noticeable?
3. Mark the derived class `final` and repeat the timing through a reference to the derived type.

cards.q: How many vtables exist for a class that has 1,000 objects?
cards.a:
One

The vtable is per class. Each object holds its own vptr, and all of them point at that single table.

Choosing the function to call at run time, by dynamic type

Early binding fixes the function while compiling. Late binding looks it up through the vptr while running.

cards.q: Why does adding five more virtual functions not increase `sizeof` the class?
cards.a:
They add vtable slots; each object still has one vptr

The extra function pointers live in the shared table, not in every object.

cards.q: Besides the indirection, what is the main performance cost of a virtual call?
cards.a:
The compiler usually cannot inline it

Without knowing the target, the compiler cannot inline the call or optimise across it. Devirtualization recovers this when the type is known.
